mcqs.question: What does the Builder in the refactored Order class actually buy, compared to incremental setters?
options: It makes field access faster at runtime
It automatically makes every field thread-local
It removes the need to copy the items list defensively
It allows the object to be constructed once and never change afterward, since there are no setters once build() returns
mcqs.explanation: The builder assembles all state before construction, then produces an object with no way to mutate it afterward. It doesn't affect field-access speed or thread-locality, and the example still defensively copies items via List.copyOf.

mcqs.question: Per the compare table, when does immutability's cost typically outweigh its benefit?
options: Whenever the object has more than one field
For a large object mutated at very high frequency on a single thread, where allocation pressure is measured to be a real problem
Whenever the object is shared across threads
For any object that's ever serialized to JSON
mcqs.explanation: High-frequency mutation of a large object is the scenario where allocation cost genuinely competes with the benefit. Thread-sharing is actually where immutability shines, and field count or JSON serialization have no bearing on the trade-off.

mcqs.question: Why isn't declaring every field final enough to guarantee true thread-safe immutability?
options: final only prevents reassigning the field itself — if it points to a mutable object like a List, and the constructor stores the caller's actual reference, that object can still be mutated from outside
final fields are re-evaluated on every thread, so they can appear different across threads
final has no effect at all on thread safety in any language
final fields require explicit synchronization to be read correctly
mcqs.explanation: final locks the reference, not the referenced object's contents — a mutable collection stored without copying is still reachable and mutable from outside. final fields don't need extra synchronization to read correctly and aren't re-evaluated per thread.

mcqs.question: A class has `final List<String> items`, set directly from the constructor's parameter with no copying. Is the class truly immutable?
options: Yes, since final on the field guarantees the reference can never be reassigned
Yes, because List objects are immutable by default in Java
No — a caller holding the original list reference passed into the constructor can still mutate it, changing the object's contents after construction
No, because final fields can't be used inside a constructor at all
mcqs.explanation: Without a defensive copy, the caller's own reference to the list still works and can mutate the shared list after construction, breaking immutability. Lists aren't immutable by default in Java, and final fields are routinely assigned in constructors.
